units.title: Quantum Foundations
units.tagline: Build the mental model for qubits, measurement, and phase.

lessons.title: Quantum Foundations

sections.text: Quantum Foundations

Quantum computing uses quantum states to process information. A classical bit is either 0 or 1; a qubit is described by amplitudes α and β with |α|² + |β|² = 1. Measurement samples an outcome and changes the state. Superposition is not uncertainty caused by missing knowledge: it is a state with multiple amplitudes. Relative phase affects interference, while global phase does not change measurement probabilities.
Pending faculty review: use this checkpoint to connect the idea to a real circuit.

checkpoints.prompt: What describes the state of a single qubit?
options: Two complex amplitudes whose squared magnitudes sum to 1
A hidden classical bit that never changes
A pair of probabilities that need not sum to 1
checkpoints.explanation: A normalized qubit state α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ has |α|² + |β|² = 1.

checkpoints.prompt: What does a computational-basis measurement tell you?
options: One sampled outcome, not every amplitude
checkpoints.explanation: Measurement returns one outcome; repeated shots estimate its probability distribution.

takeaways: Connect the mathematical model to a testable prediction.
Use a small example to check your reasoning.

lessons.title: Qubits and measurement

sections.text: Qubits and measurement

For |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, measuring in the computational basis returns 0 with probability |α|² and 1 with probability |β|². Repeating the experiment estimates these probabilities; one shot does not reveal the whole state. The Bloch sphere is a geometric representation of a pure single-qubit state, with poles for |0⟩ and |1⟩ and phase represented around the equator.
Pending faculty review: use this checkpoint to connect the idea to a real circuit.

checkpoints.prompt: For |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, what is the probability of measuring 1?
checkpoints.explanation: Born's rule squares the magnitude of the amplitude for the measured outcome.

checkpoints.prompt: Why run the same circuit many times?
options: To estimate outcome probabilities from samples
To reveal all amplitudes in one shot
To prevent measurement from changing a state
To remove every source of noise
checkpoints.explanation: Repeated shots produce a histogram that estimates the measurement distribution.

takeaways: Connect the mathematical model to a testable prediction.
Use a small example to check your reasoning.

lessons.title: Phase and interference

sections.text: Phase and interference

Two states can have the same measurement probabilities but different relative phase. A later gate can make their amplitudes add or cancel. This is the engine of many algorithms: computation arranges interference so useful answers become more likely. A global phase e^{iγ}|ψ⟩ is physically unobservable, but a relative phase between basis states is observable through interference.
Pending faculty review: use this checkpoint to connect the idea to a real circuit.

checkpoints.prompt: Two states have identical basis probabilities but different relative phase. What can distinguish them?
options: A later gate can make their amplitudes interfere differently
Nothing; relative phase is always unobservable
checkpoints.explanation: Relative phase affects interference after subsequent operations.

checkpoints.prompt: Which phase has no observable effect on measurement probabilities?
options: A global phase shared by the whole state
A relative phase between basis states
Any phase before an H gate
checkpoints.explanation: Multiplying the entire state by e^{iγ} is a global phase and does not change physical predictions.

takeaways: Connect the mathematical model to a testable prediction.

units.title: Gates and Circuits
units.tagline: Read, build, and reason about quantum circuits.

lessons.title: Gate toolkit

sections.text: Gate toolkit

Quantum gates are reversible unitary transformations. X swaps |0⟩ and |1⟩; H maps |0⟩ to (|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2; Z changes the phase of |1⟩. Y and rotations add other axes of control. Unitary means U†U=I, so the operation preserves total probability and has an inverse.
Pending faculty review: use this checkpoint to connect the idea to a real circuit.

checkpoints.prompt: What does X do to |0⟩?
checkpoints.explanation: X is the quantum NOT gate and swaps |0⟩ and |1⟩.

checkpoints.prompt: What is H|0⟩?
checkpoints.explanation: Hadamard puts |0⟩ into an equal superposition with positive relative phase.

takeaways: Connect the mathematical model to a testable prediction.
Use a small example to check your reasoning.

lessons.title: Reading circuits

sections.text: Reading circuits

A circuit diagram is a timeline for qubits. Wires are qubit registers and gates act at a moment in time. A controlled gate applies an operation only when a control condition is met. Read barriers carefully: gates on different qubits may be parallel, but measurement is not an ordinary reversible gate.
Pending faculty review: use this checkpoint to connect the idea to a real circuit.

checkpoints.prompt: In the circuit convention used here, which way does time flow?
options: It depends on the gate color
checkpoints.explanation: Read gates along each wire from left to right.

checkpoints.prompt: Can gates on separate qubits occur in the same circuit layer?
options: Yes, when they act in parallel
No, every gate must be sequential
Only if they are both X gates
checkpoints.explanation: Operations on independent wires can share a time step.

takeaways: Connect the mathematical model to a testable prediction.
Use a small example to check your reasoning.

lessons.title: Multi-qubit gates

sections.text: Multi-qubit gates

Multi-qubit systems use tensor products. CNOT flips the target when the control is 1; applied after H, it can create a Bell state. CZ changes a phase when both qubits are 1. SWAP exchanges states. These gates let circuits create correlations that cannot be represented as independent single-qubit states.
Pending faculty review: use this checkpoint to connect the idea to a real circuit.

checkpoints.prompt: What does CNOT do when its control is |0⟩?
checkpoints.explanation: CNOT flips the target only when the control is |1⟩.

checkpoints.prompt: How can H on q0 followed by CNOT(q0, q1) act on |00⟩?
checkpoints.explanation: H creates two branches and CNOT correlates q1 with q0.

takeaways: Connect the mathematical model to a testable prediction.
Use a small example to check your reasoning.

units.title: Entanglement
units.tagline: Understand tensor products, Bell states, and teleportation.

lessons.title: Bell states

sections.text: Bell states

Starting from |00⟩, a Hadamard on the first qubit creates (|00⟩ + |10⟩)/√2. A CNOT with q0 as control and q1 as target maps the second branch to |11⟩, preparing |Φ+⟩ = (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2. This joint state cannot be written as a product of single-qubit states.
Pending faculty review: use this checkpoint to connect the idea to a real circuit.

checkpoints.prompt: Which sequence prepares (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 from |00⟩?
checkpoints.explanation: H creates a superposition on q0; CNOT copies that branch value into q1.

takeaways: Connect the mathematical model to a testable prediction.
Use a small example to check your reasoning.

lessons.title: Measurement correlations

sections.text: Measurement correlations

Measuring either qubit of |Φ+⟩ alone gives a random 0 or 1. Measuring both in the computational basis gives only 00 or 11, with equal probability. The correlation is in the joint distribution; it does not let either observer choose an outcome or send a message.
Pending faculty review: use this checkpoint to connect the idea to a real circuit.

checkpoints.prompt: For |Φ+⟩ = (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2, what happens when both qubits are measured in the computational basis?
options: All four outcomes are equally likely
checkpoints.explanation: The state contains only the 00 and 11 branches, each with probability 1/2.

takeaways: Connect the mathematical model to a testable prediction.
Use a small example to check your reasoning.

lessons.title: Teleportation

sections.text: Teleportation

Quantum teleportation uses a shared Bell pair, a joint operation, measurements and two classical bits. The sender's unknown state is destroyed by measurement; the receiver applies a correction determined by the classical message. The protocol transfers a state description without copying it or sending matter faster than light.
Pending faculty review: use this checkpoint to connect the idea to a real circuit.

checkpoints.prompt: What does quantum teleportation transfer?
options: An unknown quantum state using shared entanglement and classical communication
A copy of an unknown state
A measurement result without a classical message
checkpoints.explanation: Teleportation reconstructs a state using entanglement plus two classical bits; it does not move matter or send information faster than light.

takeaways: Connect the mathematical model to a testable prediction.
Use a small example to check your reasoning.

u1.prompt: For |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, what is the probability of measuring 1?
u1.explanation: Born's rule squares the magnitude of the amplitude: P(1) = |β|².

u1.prompt: After applying H to |0⟩, what is P(|1⟩)?
u1.explanation: H|0⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2, so both outcomes have probability 1/2.

u1.prompt: Which phase cannot change observable measurement probabilities?
options: A global phase on the whole state
A relative phase between basis states
A phase on one basis state
u1.explanation: A global phase multiplies every amplitude equally and has no observable effect.

u2.prompt: When does CNOT flip its target?
u2.explanation: CNOT applies X to the target conditioned on the control being |1⟩.

u2.prompt: What state results from H on q0 then CNOT(q0,q1) applied to |00⟩?
u2.explanation: H creates two branches and CNOT correlates the second qubit with the first.

u3.prompt: What is the defining property of an entangled pure state?
options: It cannot be factored into independent states for each subsystem
u3.explanation: Entanglement means the joint state cannot be written as a product of individual subsystem states.

u3.prompt: For the Bell state (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2, if q0 is measured as 0, what is q1?
u3.explanation: The outcomes are perfectly correlated: observing 0 on q0 leaves q1 at 0.

u3.prompt: Can entanglement alone send a controllable message faster than light?
options: Yes, by choosing a Bell state
u3.explanation: Entanglement creates correlations, but the local measurement result is random and cannot carry a chosen message.

u4.prompt: What role does an oracle play in a query algorithm?
options: It guarantees an answer in one step
u4.explanation: The oracle represents the problem-specific function queried by the algorithm.

u5.prompt: What speedup does ideal Grover search provide over unstructured classical search?
options: It solves every search in one step
u5.explanation: Grover reduces query complexity from O(N) to O(√N), a quadratic speedup.

u6.prompt: What is optimized in a variational quantum algorithm?
options: Parameters of a circuit using a classical feedback loop
u6.explanation: A classical optimizer updates circuit parameters based on measured objective values.

u7.prompt: T1 primarily describes what in a superconducting qubit?
u7.explanation: T1 is the characteristic energy-relaxation time.

options: To detect and correct errors without directly measuring the encoded logical state
To eliminate the need for repeated measurements
To turn quantum data into classical copies
u7.explanation: Error-correcting codes use redundant physical qubits and syndrome measurements to protect logical information.

u8.prompt: What should you record to make a circuit experiment reproducible?
options: Circuit, input state, measurement setup and run settings
u8.explanation: A useful experiment record includes the circuit and conditions that produced the results.

u9.prompt: What does a cryostat do in a superconducting quantum computer?
options: Cools the processor to cryogenic temperatures
u9.explanation: Superconducting processors operate at very low temperatures to reduce thermal excitations.

glossary.superposition: A quantum state represented by a weighted combination of basis states.
glossary.oracle: A circuit component that encodes a function without revealing it directly.
glossary.fidelity: A measure of how close a prepared state is to a target state.
glossary.attenuation: Reduction of signal power, commonly used to thermalize cryogenic lines.
